name: Uma Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Uma, 43, with a master’s in music. I lead a small studio string team, play violin for local films, record short guide parts for schools and teach five advanced pupils. I can hear when two takes will not sit together and help the players fix it; I still practise my own part before calling anyone else in. I like the moment a messy recording becomes music, and I dislike unpaid revisions after a client approves a take.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the family depend on from those sessions?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner designs building plans on a regular salary, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage, my music pay is high for this work and about eleven months of expenses are saved. There are plenty of other music jobs nearby, although a listing is not a signed offer. I use AI daily for calendar messages and draft rehearsal notes, then check every paid date and note myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the players that a tidier calendar is helpful if the session fee stays beside the date. A violinist still has to listen when a film scene changes shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our eleven-month reserve and my partner’s salary make a delayed guide fee manageable. I still want revision limits in writing, because a small late change can use a full paid morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the studio dates and five pupils this term. This week I’d check signed recording dates and revision limits, then save a quarter of each cleared extra guide fee after mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm in this mild world. A slow invoice would be a nuisance, not a reason to miss the children’s school payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a revision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A film client once wanted a new violin ending after approving the first cut. I sent a new price before asking the team to record again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What AI do you trust already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it for calendar messages and rough rehearsal notes. I still play a part before sending it to a pupil.

I would ask clients for written **revision limits**.
think: Our **eleven-month reserve** and partner salary cover a slow guide fee.
An unpriced **late revision** can use a paid morning.
do: Keep **studio sessions** and five pupils this term.
Confirm **recording dates** and limits; save a quarter of cleared extra guide fees after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** because current pay and savings cover routine delay.
S0.quote: A violinist still has to listen when a film scene changes shape.
fieldNote: Her **senior skill** and high pay support a substantial reserve without eliminating fee disputes.
She uses **AI daily** for messages and notes, then checks parts by playing.

steps.text: Keep paid studio dates and five pupils this term
Save quarter of cleared extra guide fees after mortgage and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the studio that generated string parts may save a client money but still remove a player’s paid session. I would ask for recording reuse and revision fees in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Film guides and arranging make about a third of my music pay. I expect some clients to buy generated parts, so our reserve would stop growing as quickly even while live sessions continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI take-comparison feature on violin files I own, after confirming paid-use terms and local storage. I’d check every suggested match by ear against the picture and printed score, keep pupils’ files out and stop if it merges notes wrongly; if guide orders fall in the first year, I’d keep paid sessions and ask clients for written reuse fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a real third of my own pay. Eleven months saved gives me time to seek paid studio work; savings cannot turn an unpaid file into income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes this different from your current AI use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My current tool helps with messages, not decisions about takes. The new checker would have to match my own violin line to the film without moving a note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a student take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would not put a child’s recording or name into a tool without written family permission and clear storage; my own take is enough.

I would warn that **generated string parts** can remove paid sessions.

Ask clients for **reuse fees** if guides fall; keep paid studio sessions.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic loss of my own recording income.
S1.quote: Eleven months saved gives me time to seek paid studio work; savings cannot turn an unpaid file into income.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** compares takes, beyond daily calendar and rehearsal-note drafting.
The **owned-file trial** uses licence, storage and manual picture/score checks before paid work.

steps.text: Learn AI take checker on owned files with paid-use/local-storage approval; compare ear/picture/score, exclude pupils

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that thinking AGI by 2028 can make school guides and film parts cheaply, while capable robot violinists come around 2031. I would ask for written session dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide and arranging fees to fall sharply in 2028, perhaps a third of my pay. We have time to search, but a good reserve does not make lost work a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d confirm studio dates and five paid pupils. In the first year after AGI arrives, if guide fees stop and film sessions shrink, I’d apply for an advertised college strings-lead role only if it accepts my master’s and experience and its written net wage after travel replaces lost pay with confirmed school pickup; I’d keep current studio and pupils until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about a substantial loss, yet I can speak to several local employers. A job listing is only a door, not a payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for another credential?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted college role requires it and a funded course or paid study time exists. I would not spend the family reserve on a guessed requirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know pickup works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can collect on early design-office days, but not every afternoon. I would confirm the rota or paid childcare before accepting a timetable.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot violinists around 2031.
I would ask for **written studio dates** before counting film pay.
think: I expect **guide and arranging fees** to fall sharply.
Our **eleven-month reserve** buys search time, not replacement wages.
do: Keep **studio and pupils** until signed college offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
Seek **posted college work** if 2028 guides stop and sessions shrink; master’s/experience accepted, written replacement net-after-travel pay and confirmed pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely lost sessions despite savings.
S2.quote: A job listing is only a door, not a payslip.
fieldNote: Thinking AGI threatens **guides and arranging** before robots play violin around 2031.
A college move needs **actual vacancy**, accepted master’s, written replacement pay and confirmed pickup.

steps.text: Keep paid studio sessions and five pupils until signed college offer
Seek posted college role if both guides/sessions fall; master's/experience accepted, replacement written net-after-travel pay, pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell clients that five years gives us time to decide which film recording work still earns a human fee. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031, and robot violinists around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a separate paid string-recording clinic, where small groups learn to record their own parts, but it would need paying adults and a proper room. I will not use the mortgage reserve to rent silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask an independent arts centre for a fixed studio fee and offer a four-session adult recording clinic only if twelve adults prepay enough for the room, my teaching and preparation, a paid sound assistant’s setup and supervision, and confirmed childcare. In the first year after 2031 I’d repeat only if twelve still pay those costs, the room is available and pickup is covered; I’d keep my paid studio dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about film fees fading within five years, though I can test a class. A full registration form is not a paid recording session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the sound assistant do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would check the microphones and supervise levels while adults play. I would pay for their setup and teaching hour before accepting a class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if eight adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund them and keep my existing pupils. Eight fees would not cover a room, an assistant and my time.

say: I would explain that **2031 thinking AGI** precedes robot violinists around 2034.
I would offer a **paid recording clinic** only with advance fees.
think: Twelve **prepaid adults** must cover the room and both teachers before a recording session begins.
The **mortgage reserve** cannot fund an unfilled studio while we still owe monthly bills.
do: Ask arts centre for a **fixed room fee** next spring; start only with twelve prepayments covering my teaching/prep, assistant setup/supervision and childcare.
Repeat **clinic** after 2031 only if twelve cover all costs, room available and pickup confirmed; keep paid studio dates.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording pay while testing a separate clinic.
S3.quote: A full registration form is not a paid recording session.
fieldNote: Her **clinic gate** includes a fixed room fee and twelve prepayments covering her time and assistant setup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that a decade is enough time to learn how a music fee is earned and written down. Thinking AGI comes around 2036 and robot violinists around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still lead the studio strings, though guide fees could be smaller. Our eleven-month reserve and my partner’s salary make the coming few years secure enough to plan patiently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep paid studio dates and five pupils and save a quarter of each cleared extra guide fee after mortgage and food, aiming for twelve months. Through the decade I’d offer the recording clinic only if twelve prepayments cover fixed room fee, my teaching/preparation, assistant setup/supervision and childcare; in the first year after 2036 I’d repeat only while those paid conditions hold and seek an advertised college lead role if guide fees end, provided my master’s qualifies and written net pay after travel replaces lost income with pickup covered, while keeping current work until signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant market for recordings, not next month’s mortgage. A fee is real when it clears the bank, not when a client says the session sounds promising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy new studio equipment now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the current gear while it works. Extra guide money goes to savings only after the fee clears and the household bills are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the clinic stops paying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the next term before the assistant works unpaid and keep the studio sessions that still pay. A full calendar does not justify a loss-making class.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide and film fees could fall before a college post opens. Written studio dates, an actual role accepting my master’s with replacement net pay, and twelve paid adults for a clinic would help. Eleven months saved gives me time to ask, not a reason to give a studio away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid when a client asks for one more violin take. A request for one more violin take can fill a musician's whole morning.
